Your Policy Is Secretly a Harness:
The Decision Geometry of Agent Interfaces

Jian Mu The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) Ruibo Shen The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) Yao Shu The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou) The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology ††thanks: Corresponding author: yaoshu@hkust-gz.edu.cn.
Abstract

Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Harnesses are often revised and judged by how an already trained model performs under them, which assumes that what the model learned under one harness carries over to the next. We ask what a policy learns from its harness and what survives when the harness changes. Under KL-regularized control, we show that the log odds of an optimal policy recover how strongly its harness favors each action over the others, so a trained policy carries the preferences of its harness. Deployed return then equals the ceiling of the harness, the best return it offers, minus the mismatch of the policy, the return lost to its own suboptimal decisions. Training changes only the mismatch, while changing the harness moves both terms. Comparing harnesses with a fixed model therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well that model uses it. In MiniWoB++, post-training makes a model’s preferences specific to its training harness. Reversing the order of the observation fields leaves every optimal decision unchanged yet lowers a trained model’s success from 85.0% to 19.2%. Conversely, every new harness that a fixed-model comparison rejects but that raises the ceiling outperforms the original agent after further training under it, and ceiling and mismatch measured beforehand predict these gains. For coding-agent harnesses on Terminal-Bench Lite, ceiling minus mismatch estimated with a stronger model as a stand-in for the optimum reproduces the accuracy ranking, while either term alone does not. Code is available at https://github.com/2020-qqtcg/HRP.

1 Introduction

Language model agents are post-trained and deployed through a harness, the prompts, tools, and control logic that present a task to the model and execute its outputs. Interface design and prompt formatting change agent performance (Yang et al., 2024; Sclar et al., 2024). Automated harness design revises prompts, tools, and workflows and scores each candidate by how a fixed model performs under it (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Fernando et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2026). Such a score assumes that what the model learned under earlier harnesses carries over to each candidate, yet the same interface change can raise one model’s accuracy and lower that of a fine-tuned model (Mu et al., 2025). At the same time, training can move behavior that a prompt or a harness supplies into the weights (Snell et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2026), and recent methods adapt harnesses and weights together (Hebbar et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). These practices raise the question we study:

What does a policy learn from its harness, and what survives when the harness changes?

Two experiments make the question concrete. In the first, we take a web agent post-trained under one harness and reverse the order of the fields in its observation, a JSON object with fields such as the task instruction, the page state, and the available actions. The fields keep their contents. We also hold fixed the actions, their execution, the rewards, and the reference policy that regularizes training, so every optimal decision stays the same. The model still changes its most probable action at about half of the states, and its task success falls from 85.0% to 19.2%. Keeping the decisions a model should make does not keep the decisions it makes.

In the second, a new harness adds batched clicks, which execute two clicks in one decision. The new actions raise the best achievable return, yet the trained model’s success drops when we move it to the new harness without changing its weights. A frozen comparison, which evaluates candidate harnesses with the same trained weights, would therefore reject the new harness. We then train the model further for the same budget under each harness, starting from the same trained weights, which we call the source checkpoint. We call further training under the new harness adaptation, and further training under the original harness continuation. The adapted model succeeds more often than both the source checkpoint and the continued one. The harness that first hurt the model gives the best agent. Figure 1 shows the task success at each step, with the new harness as Harness 1.

We explain both results in the control problem that a harness induces over semantic actions, the operations an agent executes together with their arguments. Under KL-regularized control, the optimal policy is a softmax over action scores. Each score adds an action’s long-term value to its log probability under the reference policy, so an optimal policy’s log odds between two actions are proportional to the difference of their scores. A policy trained to optimality under a harness therefore carries the relative action scores that the harness induces, even though it contains none of the harness’s code, tools, or execution machinery. In this sense, a policy is secretly a harness. In our controlled study, real post-training moves a model’s action scores toward the optimum of its training harness, and each harness leaves its own preferences in the model.

Action scores also show why a trained policy can fail after it is moved to a new harness. The scores a policy carries are the ones it expresses through its training interface, which we call its readout through that interface, and the same weights can express different scores through another interface. A policy is thus secretly its training harness, as read through that harness. A new harness can therefore change which actions are optimal, by moving the optimal scores, and separately change which actions the model picks, by moving the readout. Reversing the observation fields leaves the optimal scores in place and moves only the readout.

Scores fix decisions but not how much return a harness offers, since raising every reward by the same constant changes no decision. To convert score changes into return, we therefore add this value back by applying the regularized performance-gap identity (Geist et al., 2019; O’Donoghue, 2022) to the harness-induced problem. Deployed return equals the harness’s ceiling CC, the best return any policy can reach under it, minus the policy’s mismatch MM, the return the policy loses by departing from the optimal policy. The mismatch is the KL divergence from the optimal policy, accumulated along the policy’s own trajectories. The ceiling does not depend on the model’s weights, so training under a fixed harness changes only MM, while a harness change can move both terms. A frozen comparison of harnesses therefore mixes what each harness offers with how well the current checkpoint uses it. In the batched-click example, the new harness raises the ceiling slightly but raises the frozen model’s mismatch about ten times as much, so return falls. Adaptation then lowers the mismatch, and once the mismatch falls below a threshold we derive, the adapted model beats the original model under the original harness. Figure 2 illustrates both steps. Our contributions are as follows.

1. What a policy learns under a harness. The log odds of an optimal policy identify exactly the relative action scores that a harness induces. These scores fix every decision but not how much return the harness offers, which Contribution 3 adds back as the ceiling. On MiniWoB++, post-training moves the model’s action preferences toward the training harness’s optimum and makes them specific to that harness.

2. Why transfer fails. We split the score error of a policy moved to a new harness into three parts. The target shift is the change in the optimal scores, the training residual is the error that training under the original harness left behind, and the readout drift is the change in the scores that the model expresses. Presentation changes that keep every optimal decision isolate the readout drift, and they alone can make a trained model fail on most tasks.

3. What transfer costs and how to measure it. Deployed return equals ceiling minus mismatch exactly. From this identity we derive the mismatch threshold below which adaptation turns a harness revision that hurt the frozen model into a gain. Adaptation to batched clicks crosses this threshold and outperforms continued training under the original harness. We also move trained checkpoints between six harnesses. Among the moves that a frozen comparison rejects, ceiling and mismatch measured before adaptation predict which ones adaptation makes beneficial. Mismatch estimated from sampled actions predicts return changes when the optimum is known. For coding agents, where no optimum is available, estimates that put a stronger teacher model in the optimum’s place order five harnesses by Terminal-Bench Lite accuracy.

2 Harnesses Induce Semantic Control Problems

A harness turns model outputs into executed operations. We call an executed operation together with its arguments a semantic action a∈𝒜a\in\mathcal{A}, such as clicking a particular element or running a query. Different outputs can execute the same action. For example, a JSON object and a function-call string may issue the same parameterized query. Let s∈𝒮s\in\mathcal{S} denote the semantic decision state. An interface ℐ=(cℐ,dℐ,eℐ)\mathcal{I}=(c_{\mathcal{I}},d_{\mathcal{I}},e_{\mathcal{I}}) formalizes a harness. It encodes the state into a context, decodes a model response into an action, and executes that action. For a token policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, the induced semantic policy sums the probabilities of the outputs that decode to the same action:

Πθ,ℐ(a∣s)=∑y:dℐ​(y,s)=aπθ(y∣cℐ(s)).\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}(a\mid s)=\sum_{y:\,d_{\mathcal{I}}(y;s)=a}\pi_{\theta}(y\mid c_{\mathcal{I}}(s)). (1)

Both the context cℐc_{\mathcal{I}} and the decoder dℐd_{\mathcal{I}} enter Eq. (1), so fixed weights do not fix the semantic policy.

Together with a fixed task environment, ℐ\mathcal{I} induces a transition law PℐP_{\mathcal{I}}, a utility rℐr_{\mathcal{I}} that includes execution costs, and a semantic reference policy πℐref\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}}. Every call to the evaluated model is a decision, including calls for verification or retry, and the state includes the harness’s controller memory, such as tool results and remaining budget. Appendix B specifies this construction and the conditions under which training over tokens yields semantic optimality.

Across comparisons, we fix the initial distribution ρ0\rho_{0}, discount 0≤γ<10\leq\gamma<1, and regularization coefficient τ>0\tau>0, and measure rewards on a common scale. Each interface’s reference is part of its control problem and does not change during training. For finite 𝒮,𝒜\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A}, bounded rewards, and πℐref​(a∣s)>0\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}}(a\mid s)>0, the regularized return of a semantic policy Π\Pi is

Jℐ​(Π)=𝔼ρ0,Π,Pℐ​[∑t≥0γt​(rℐ​(st,at)−τ​log⁡Π⁡(at∣st)πℐref​(at∣st))].J_{\mathcal{I}}(\Pi)=\mathbb{E}_{\rho_{0},\Pi,P_{\mathcal{I}}}\!\left[\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\left(r_{\mathcal{I}}(s_{t},a_{t})-\tau\log\frac{\Pi(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}{\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}\right)\right]. (2)

Write Πℐ∗\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}} for the optimal policy and dℐΠ​(s)=(1−γ)​∑t≥0γt​PrℐΠ⁡(st=s)d^{\Pi}_{\mathcal{I}}(s)=(1-\gamma)\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\Pr_{\mathcal{I}}^{\Pi}(s_{t}=s) for the discounted occupancy of Π\Pi.

Controlled study.

In our mechanism experiments, every quantity above can be computed exactly. Six harnesses act on three MiniWoB++ task families (Liu et al., 2018), and we compile each induced control problem into a finite graph. H0 executes one native action per decision, and H1–H5 add batched clicks, automatic checks, verification tools, or extra instructions. Each prompt lists the complete action menu with one token per action, so the model’s next-token distribution gives Πθ,ℐ\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}} exactly. The reward is binary task success. We post-train Qwen3.5-2B with exact policy gradients, and the frozen base model serves as the reference. A soft Bellman solve gives each harness’s optimum. Evaluations use tasks held out from training, and Appendix F.1 gives the full protocol.

3 What a Policy Learns under a Harness

We now ask what a model’s action probabilities reveal about the control problem it was trained on.

3.1 Optimal Policies Encode Relative Action Scores

The optimal action value Qℐ∗Q^{*}_{\mathcal{I}} depends on the harness’s utility and transition law through the soft Bellman equations, and the optimal policy takes the Gibbs form Πℐ∗​(a∣s)∝πℐref​(a∣s)​exp⁡(Qℐ∗​(s,a)/τ)\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(a\mid s)\propto\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}}(a\mid s)\exp(Q^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(s,a)/\tau) (Haarnoja et al., 2017; Geist et al., 2019). An action’s optimal probability therefore depends on its long-term value and its reference probability. We combine the two into the optimal action score

Fℐ∗(s,a)=Qℐ∗(s,a)+τlogπℐref(a∣s),Πℐ∗(⋅∣s)=softmax(Fℐ∗(s,⋅)/τ).F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(s,a)=Q^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(s,a)+\tau\log\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}}(a\mid s),\qquad\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(\cdot\mid s)=\operatorname{softmax}\bigl(F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(s,\cdot)/\tau\bigr). (3)

For instance, an optimal policy may favor a batch of clicks because the batch leads to better outcomes or because the reference places more weight on it. The score records the combined effect.

Adding the same constant to every action’s score at a state leaves the policy unchanged, so only score differences within a state affect decisions. We write [F][F] for the class of score fields related by such statewise constants. Two interfaces have equivalent optimal decisions when Πℐ1∗(⋅∣s)=Πℐ2∗(⋅∣s)\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{1}}(\cdot\mid s)=\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{2}}(\cdot\mid s) at every aligned state, that is, every semantic state that the two interfaces share.

Proposition 3.1 (Behavioral identification).

Two interfaces have equivalent optimal decisions if and only if [Fℐ1∗]=[Fℐ2∗][F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{1}}]=[F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{2}}]. If a checkpoint is optimal for its training interface at every semantic state, then

[τ​log⁡Πθ,ℐtr]=[Fℐtr∗],τ​log⁡Πθ,ℐtr​(a∣s)Πθ,ℐtr​(b∣s)=Fℐtr∗​(s,a)−Fℐtr∗​(s,b).[\tau\log\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}]=[F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}],\qquad\tau\log\frac{\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}(a\mid s)}{\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}(b\mid s)}=F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}(s,a)-F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}(s,b). (4)

Behavior determines exactly these relative scores. Different reference policies, rewards, and even transition laws can share one optimal score field and therefore one optimal policy, in line with partial identifiability results for reward learning (Skalse et al., 2023). Behavior also leaves absolute value undetermined, since adding a constant to every reward raises the optimal return and changes no decision. A policy can thus carry the decisions a harness induces without its code, tools, or execution machinery. The value a harness offers is a separate quantity, which Section 5 adds back. Appendix C proves the proposition from the Gibbs form and constructs such mechanisms.

A real checkpoint departs from the optimum. To compare the two, we represent each class by its centered member, subtracting the mean score across actions at each state: F¯=P⟂​F\bar{F}=P_{\!\perp}F with P⟂=I−𝟏𝟏⊤/nP_{\!\perp}=I-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}/n and n=|𝒜|n=|\mathcal{A}|. For positive semantic probabilities, the checkpoint’s centered scores are F^θ,ℐ=τ​P⟂​log⁡Πθ,ℐ\widehat{F}_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}=\tau P_{\!\perp}\log\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}, the scores whose softmax in Eq. (3) reproduces the checkpoint’s own policy. We call them the model’s readout through ℐ\mathcal{I}, the action preferences it expresses through the interface. Its score error under the training interface, etr=F^θ,ℐtr−F¯ℐtr∗e_{\rm tr}=\widehat{F}_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}-\bar{F}^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}, vanishes exactly when the checkpoint is optimal.

3.2 Post-Training Makes Preferences Harness-Specific

Proposition 3.1 concerns optimal policies. We ask whether real post-training moves a model toward the optimum of its training harness, and whether what it learns depends on that harness. We post-train Qwen3.5-2B under each of H0–H5. The geometry error of a checkpoint is the mean squared difference between its centered scores and the optimal ones, averaged over a fixed bank of reachable states, so that every checkpoint is scored on the same decisions.

Under every harness, post-training raises task success, and the geometry error falls well below its initial level, by 69% to 90% by the end of training. It falls as much on held-out tasks that play no role in the updates as on training tasks. The model learns effective task behavior while its action scores approach the optimum of its training harness.

To test whether the learned preferences depend on the training harness, we deploy each final checkpoint under all six harnesses on test tasks. A fixed deployment harness fixes the dynamics, reference, and optimal scores, so the six checkpoints are compared against the same target. Under every deployment harness, the checkpoint trained under that harness has the lowest error. Post-training thus makes the model’s preferences specific to its training harness. Figure 3 shows the learning curves in its first two panels and this comparison in the third.

4 Why Policy Transfer Fails

Section 3 shows that a trained policy carries the relative action scores of its training harness. It carries them in its readout through the training interface rather than independently of that interface, so the same weights need not express the same preferences under another harness. A harness change can therefore break a policy that has learned its training harness well.

4.1 A Harness Change Moves the Target and the Readout

Let interfaces 11 and 22 be the training and deployment interfaces. A change in execution can change which actions are optimal, and a change in presentation can change which actions the frozen model selects. On aligned states and actions, the deployed score error splits into three terms:

F^θ,2−F¯2∗⏟deployed error=F¯1∗−F¯2∗⏟g12:target shift+F^θ,1−F¯1∗⏟e1:training residual+F^θ,2−F^θ,1⏟η12:readout drift.\underbrace{\widehat{F}_{\theta,2}-\bar{F}^{*}_{2}}_{\text{deployed error}}=\underbrace{\bar{F}^{*}_{1}-\bar{F}^{*}_{2}}_{g_{12}:\ \text{target shift}}+\underbrace{\widehat{F}_{\theta,1}-\bar{F}^{*}_{1}}_{e_{1}:\ \text{training residual}}+\underbrace{\widehat{F}_{\theta,2}-\widehat{F}_{\theta,1}}_{\eta_{12}:\ \text{readout drift}}. (5)

The training residual exists before the change, and the target shift and the readout drift are its two effects. They are vectors, so they can add up or cancel.

4.2 Equivalent Optimal Decisions, Different Behavior

When two interfaces have equivalent optimal decisions, g12=0g_{12}=0, and any change in the model’s error comes from readout drift. We test this with the H0-trained checkpoint. We reverse the order of the observation fields, render the action menu as a list, or reassign the action codes, and keep the transitions, rewards, and semantic reference fixed, so neither the target nor the reference can move. The optimal policy and the optimal return thus stay the same, as numerical checks confirm.

Equivalent optimal decisions do not produce equivalent behavior. Reversing the field order has the largest effect. It changes the model’s most probable action at about half of the states, and most tasks then fail. Reassigning the action codes has a moderate effect, and the list format has a small one. Unlike earlier studies of prompt-format sensitivity (Sclar et al., 2024), the control problem here certifies that the optimal policy is unchanged, so the entire effect comes from the model’s readout. Table 1 lists the results, Appendix F.2 gives the protocol, and Appendix D.4 bounds readout drift by the model’s sensitivity to corresponding outputs.

5 What Transfer Costs and When Adaptation Recovers It

Separating the two changes shows what moved. What they cost in return depends on which decisions they affect and how often the policy reaches them.

5.1 From Score Errors to Lost Return

Consider a single decision at state ss in a fixed interface ℐ\mathcal{I}. If the policy Π\Pi makes this decision and the optimal policy makes every later one, the return lost relative to acting optimally throughout is τKL(Π(⋅∣s)∥Πℐ∗(⋅∣s))\tau\mathrm{KL}(\Pi(\cdot\mid s)\|\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(\cdot\mid s)). If Π\Pi also makes the later decisions, each of them adds its own loss, and summing along the trajectories of Π\Pi gives the total gap (O’Donoghue, 2022).

Proposition 5.1 (Regularized performance gap).

For any semantic policy Π\Pi in a fixed interface,

Jℐ(Πℐ∗)−Jℐ(Π)=τ1−γ𝔼s∼dℐΠKL(Π(⋅∣s)∥Πℐ∗(⋅∣s)).J_{\mathcal{I}}(\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}})-J_{\mathcal{I}}(\Pi)=\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{s\sim d^{\Pi}_{\mathcal{I}}}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(\Pi(\cdot\mid s)\|\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(\cdot\mid s)\bigr). (6)

The occupancy weights each local loss by how often the evaluated policy reaches the state, so errors on the policy’s common paths cost the most. In terms of scores, the local loss is the Bregman divergence DΦ​(F,G)D_{\Phi}(F,G) of Φ⁡(F)=τ​log​∑aeFa/τ\Phi(F)=\tau\log\sum_{a}e^{F_{a}/\tau}, a smooth maximum of the scores. DΦ​(F,G)D_{\Phi}(F,G) is the gap between Φ⁡(F)\Phi(F) and the linear approximation of Φ\Phi at GG. For positive semantic action probabilities,

τKL(Πθ,ℐ∥Πℐ∗)=DΦ(Fℐ∗,F^θ,ℐ).\tau\mathrm{KL}(\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}\|\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}})=D_{\Phi}(F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}},\widehat{F}_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}). (7)

The scores of the actions at a state locate the model’s decision, and DΦD_{\Phi} measures how much return the decision loses when the model’s scores sit at F^θ,ℐ\widehat{F}_{\theta,\mathcal{I}} instead of Fℐ∗F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}. We call these scores and this cost together the decision geometry of a harness. Averaging DΦD_{\Phi} under the deployed policy’s occupancy turns the score error of Eq. (5) into lost return. For small errors, DΦD_{\Phi} grows roughly quadratically with the summed error, so the three terms of Eq. (5) cost return through their sum rather than one by one, and Proposition 6.1 below turns this into a bound. Appendix D proves both identities.

5.2 Ceiling and Mismatch

Relative scores fix the decisions and leave the value of a harness undetermined. We add that value back. Define the ceiling C⁡(ℐ)=Jℐ​(Πℐ∗)C(\mathcal{I})=J_{\mathcal{I}}(\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}), the optimal regularized return of the harness and thus the best that any policy can reach under it, and the mismatch M⁡(θ,ℐ)M(\theta,\mathcal{I}), the return the checkpoint leaves unrealized. Proposition 5.1 gives

Jℐ(Πθ,ℐ)=C(ℐ)−M(θ,ℐ),M(θ,ℐ)=τ1−γ𝔼dℐΠθ,ℐKL(Πθ,ℐ∥Πℐ∗).J_{\mathcal{I}}(\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}})=C(\mathcal{I})-M(\theta,\mathcal{I}),\qquad M(\theta,\mathcal{I})=\frac{\tau}{1-\gamma}\mathbb{E}_{d^{\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}}\mathrm{KL}(\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}\|\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}). (8)

The ceiling depends on the harness and the objective, and the mismatch depends on the harness and the checkpoint, including errors inherited from training. With the harness fixed, a weight update changes return only through MM, and a harness change can move both terms. In the summit illustration of Figure 2, the step from ① to ② is a harness revision, and the step from ② to ③ is a weight update. We call a checkpoint together with the harness it is deployed under a pair. For a frozen checkpoint, write JjJ_{j}, CjC_{j}, and MjM_{j} for the quantities under interface jj. Then

J2−J1=(C2−C1)−(M2−M1),J_{2}-J_{1}=(C_{2}-C_{1})-(M_{2}-M_{1}), (9)

so a revision helps a frozen model only when its ceiling gain exceeds the added mismatch. In the presentation study, the ceiling is fixed, so each increase in mismatch appears as an equal loss in return. Table 1 reports both for each presentation.

5.3 When Adaptation Makes a Revision Beneficial

When a revision raises the ceiling but lowers the frozen model’s return, adapting to it can realize the gain, since every unit of mismatch removed adds a unit of return. Write J⁡(θ,ℐ)=Jℐ​(Πθ,ℐ)J(\theta,\mathcal{I})=J_{\mathcal{I}}(\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}).

Corollary 5.2 (Adaptation after a harmful revision).

Let θ0\theta_{0} be the source checkpoint, trained under ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1}, let θ1\theta_{1} be the checkpoint adapted from it under ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2}, and let Δ​C=C2−C1\Delta C=C_{2}-C_{1}. Suppose the revision harms the frozen source checkpoint, J⁡(θ0,ℐ2)<J⁡(θ0,ℐ1)J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{2})<J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}). The adapted pair outperforms the source pair, J⁡(θ1,ℐ2)>J⁡(θ0,ℐ1)J(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2})>J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}), if and only if

M⁡(θ1,ℐ2)<C2−J⁡(θ0,ℐ1)=Δ​C+M⁡(θ0,ℐ1).M(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2})<C_{2}-J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1})=\Delta C+M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}). (10)

The threshold T=Δ​C+M⁡(θ0,ℐ1)T=\Delta C+M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}) is the new ceiling minus the source pair’s return. In words, adaptation pays off once the mismatch left under the new harness is smaller than the ceiling gain plus the mismatch that the source pair already had. Three comparisons describe the outcome. Recovery compares the adapted pair with the source pair, harness ranking compares the two harnesses at the adapted checkpoint, and gain over continuation compares adaptation with continued training under the source harness at the same budget, which tests whether the benefit comes from the revision or from further training. Appendix D.6 proves the corollary, and Appendix D.5 illustrates reversal and adaptation in a two-action example.

Batched clicks.

From the H0-trained checkpoint, we create two branches with identical weights, update budgets, and task draws. One continues training under H0, and the other adapts to H1, which adds batched clicks. H1 raises the ceiling slightly, but the frozen checkpoint carries its H0 preferences into H1 and adds far more mismatch, so return and task success fall. Adaptation under H1 removes most of this mismatch, while the H0 branch, which never trains under H1, keeps it. During adaptation, the checkpoint’s return under H1 rises and its return under H0 falls. Its ranking of the two harnesses therefore reverses first, and only later does it beat the source pair. At the end, the adapted pair beats both the source pair and the H0 branch in task success and in return, and the paired intervals of these differences exclude zero. Figure 4 shows both branches in its first panel, and Appendix F.3 gives the endpoint measurements.

Across harness swaps.

Batched clicks are one of many possible swaps among H0–H5. A swap moves the checkpoint post-trained under a source harness to a different target harness. We adapt every swap that a frozen comparison rejects and whose TT is positive. When T≤0T\leq 0, no policy under the target harness can beat the source pair, since mismatch is never negative. Nine swaps meet both conditions. After adaptation, the seven that raise the ceiling all beat the source pair, and the two that lower it gain nothing. Three of the seven switch to H5, which only adds instructions, so a revision that changes no action can still raise the ceiling through the reference it induces.

The frozen loss says little about this final gain. H0→\toH5 and H4→\toH3 lose the same small amount when frozen, yet H0→\toH5 ties for the largest gain and H4→\toH3 gains nothing. H0→\toH1 has the largest frozen loss and still gains. The frozen return change, T−M⁡(θ0,ℐ2)T-M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{2}), and the gain, T−M⁡(θ1,ℐ2)T-M(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2}), differ only in the mismatch under the target harness, the target mismatch. Before adaptation, the target mismatch reflects preferences learned under the source harness and varies widely across swaps. Adaptation removes most of it, so the gain follows TT, which differs across swaps mainly through the ceiling gain.

Ceiling and mismatch can therefore predict each gain before adaptation. Let r2r_{2} be the mismatch of the checkpoint post-trained directly under the target harness, measured under that harness. If adaptation brings the target mismatch down to this same level, the gain is T−r2T-r_{2}. This prediction needs only the oracle ceilings and the six post-training runs of Section 3.2. We recorded it before adaptation for every swap except H0→\toH1. It gets the sign of every gain right and orders the eight recorded gains with Spearman ρ=0.95\rho=0.95, while the frozen return change orders them with ρ=0.17\rho=0.17. Figure 4 plots the gains against the frozen return change in its second panel and against T−r2T-r_{2} in its third, and Appendix F.4 lists all nine swaps with their rank correlations.

6 Measuring Mismatch in Deployment

The results so far use full action distributions and a solved optimum. A deployed agent exposes only sampled actions and may have no known optimum, so we estimate mismatch from action samples, first against a known optimal policy and then against a teacher model in its place.

6.1 Estimating Mismatch from Action Samples

Measuring mismatch requires the optimal policy, or a stand-in for it, and action samples that the deployed model draws through its unchanged interface at states on its own trajectories, since mismatch weights each decision by how often the model reaches it.

Pilot rollouts supply these states. Stopping each rollout at a random time tt drawn with probability (1−γ)​γt(1-\gamma)\gamma^{t} gives an exact draw from discounted occupancy. At each of mm such states, we sample NN actions through the deployed interface and smooth the counts into an action distribution p~(⋅∣s)\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid s). The mismatch estimate averages the KL divergence over the sampled states:

M^=τ(1−γ)​m∑i=1mKL(p~(⋅∣si)∥Πℐ∗(⋅∣si)).\widehat{M}=\frac{\tau}{(1-\gamma)m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid s_{i})\middle\|\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(\cdot\mid s_{i})\right). (11)

A second route needs the probabilities of only the queried actions. The scaled log odds between two actions, τ​log⁡[Πθ,ℐ​(a∣s)/Πθ,ℐ​(b∣s)]\tau\log[\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}(a\mid s)/\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}(b\mid s)], equal the difference of their scores in the model’s readout. If the queried pairs link every action to every other through a chain of pairs, these differences determine all centered scores. Comparing them with the optimal scores gives the centered score error, which bounds the mismatch.

Proposition 6.1 (From score error to mismatch).

Let xs=F^θ,ℐ​(s,⋅)−F¯ℐ∗​(s,⋅)x_{s}=\widehat{F}_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}(s,\cdot)-\bar{F}^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(s,\cdot) and εd2=𝔼dℐΠθ,ℐ​‖xs‖22\varepsilon_{d}^{2}=\mathbb{E}_{d^{\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}}\left\lVert x_{s}\right\rVert_{2}^{2}. For positive semantic action probabilities,

M⁡(θ,ℐ)≤εd24​τ​(1−γ).M(\theta,\mathcal{I})\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{d}^{2}}{4\tau(1-\gamma)}. (12)

Once this bound falls below the threshold in Corollary 5.2, the adapted pair is guaranteed to outperform the source pair. Appendix E gives the proof and a lower bound on mismatch. Section 6.2 tests the sampled estimate M^\widehat{M} against a known optimum, and Section 6.3 applies the score-error bound with a teacher model in the optimum’s place.

6.2 Finite Measurements Predict Return Changes

Section 5 computed every mismatch exactly. We now ask whether the sampled estimate M^\widehat{M} of Eq. (11) can replace it, both for large return changes and for the small differences that decide whether adaptation pays off. An oracle supplies the ceiling and the optimal action distributions, and the deployed model is accessed only through sampled actions. The predicted return change of a candidate relative to its baseline is Δ​J^=Δ​C−Δ​M^\widehat{\Delta J}=\Delta C-\Delta\widehat{M}, and exact returns on tasks and configurations held out from calibrating the estimator serve as ground truth. We compare this prediction with two baselines at the same query budget. The ceiling alone sets Δ​M^=0\Delta\widehat{M}=0. A frequency rollout estimates each return directly by running the policy and estimating each selected action’s log probability from repeated queries.

Large changes across configurations.

We deploy the final H0-trained and H1-adapted checkpoints through H0’s native actions and vary one aspect of the deployment at a time, namely how reliably a click executes, what a click costs, or how the prompt is presented. We predict each configuration’s return change relative to a fixed baseline configuration. The ceiling alone fails, because presentation changes move the mismatch and leave the ceiling fixed. Subtracting the sampled mismatch reduces the prediction error about a hundredfold and gets the direction of every change not close to zero. The frequency rollout is about as accurate, so on large changes the two estimators perform alike.

Small differences during adaptation.

Recovery and harness ranking from Section 5.3 are differences of a few hundredths in return, and their signs decide whether adaptation pays off. We predict both at each saved H1-adapted checkpoint. Here the mismatch-based prediction is about ten times more accurate than the frequency rollout. It takes the ceiling difference from the oracle and estimates only the mismatch, whereas the rollout estimates the full return of each pair. The predicted ranking reverses at the same checkpoint as the observed one, and the predicted recovery comes one saved checkpoint later. The frequency rollout overestimates both differences and predicts the reversal too early. Figure 5 shows both predictions, and Appendices F.5 and F.6 give the sampling budget and all numerical results.

6.3 Ceiling and Mismatch of Coding-Agent Harnesses

We deploy a frozen Qwen3.5-9B through the native configurations of five coding-agent harnesses: DeepAgents, Pi coding-agent, DeepSeek Harness, Terminus-2, and mini-SWE-agent. With the model fixed, the harness moves Terminal-Bench Lite accuracy from 47.9% to 64.1%. We ask whether the ceiling and the mismatch explain this ordering.

Teacher-based estimates.

Coding agents have open action spaces and no solvable optimum, so a stronger teacher model, GPT-5.6-luna, takes the optimum’s place. Below, the evaluated model means the frozen Qwen3.5-9B. On three Terminal-Bench Lite tasks, we record every decision of the evaluated model, sample outputs from it and from the teacher through the unchanged harness, and map each output to an action category shared by all harnesses, such as inspecting files, modifying them, running commands, or planning. We use the evaluated model’s own category distribution as the reference. Its KL penalty is then zero, so its regularized return equals its success probability, and by Eq. (8) so does its exact ceiling minus mismatch. We estimate the ceiling by the teacher’s regularized return, C~\widetilde{C}. We estimate the mismatch, M~\widetilde{M}, with the bound of Proposition 6.1, using the teacher’s log odds in place of the optimal scores and summing along the evaluated model’s trajectories. Because the teacher is not optimal, we test whether the estimates order the harnesses by accuracy. Appendix F.7 gives the protocol and estimators.

C~−M~\widetilde{C}-\widetilde{M} orders the harnesses.

Computed without the evaluated model’s task outcomes, C~−M~\widetilde{C}-\widetilde{M} orders all five harnesses as accuracy does. Either term alone misorders them. The ceiling estimate alone ranks mini-SWE-agent first, and the mismatch estimate alone ranks Pi coding-agent second, while their difference ranks both correctly. Terminus-2 has a middle ceiling and leads through the smallest mismatch. DeepSeek Harness and mini-SWE-agent have the two highest ceilings and large mismatch, the profile of the batched-click harness before adaptation. Table 6 lists the estimates.

The same pattern appears when both terms are exact. On MiniWoB++, where they can be computed, we let a frozen Qwen3.5-9B serve as its own reference under H0–H5. The ceiling alone then ranks the most successful harness last, and the mismatch alone ranks H0 below two less successful harnesses, while only their difference orders all six correctly. Appendix F.8 gives this comparison.

Where mismatch comes from.

By Proposition 5.1, mismatch accumulates along the model’s own trajectories, so it grows with the number of decisions a harness asks of the model. DeepAgents has a mismatch per decision close to that of Terminus-2, but the evaluated model makes nearly three times as many model calls under it and accumulates the largest mismatch. DeepSeek Harness has the largest mismatch per decision. Under it, the teacher plans much more often than the evaluated model, and the evaluated model inspects the environment much more often. Figure 6 separates the two factors for each harness.

7 Discussion and Conclusion

A policy trained under a harness learns the harness’s relative action scores and expresses them through its interface. Post-training makes these preferences harness-specific, and a new interface can change the model’s choices even when every optimal decision stays the same. Because deployed return is the ceiling minus the mismatch, a harness that offers more can hurt a trained model and become the best choice after adaptation. Mismatch estimated from sampled actions predicts these changes when the optimum is known, and for coding agents, teacher-based estimates of ceiling minus mismatch order harnesses by accuracy. Harness evaluations should therefore report the ceiling next to the frozen return, evaluate several checkpoints under each harness rather than a single one, and check how presentation changes move the model’s choices. Harness distillation and joint adaptation of harnesses and weights (Ye et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026) can use sampled-action measurements to track the ceiling and the mismatch separately. Appendix A discusses related work.

Appendix A Related Work

Regularized control and decision geometry. Control as inference and RL with a maximum entropy objective express optimal policies through rewards, action values, and reference distributions (Levine, 2018; Haarnoja et al., 2017; Haarnoja et al., 2018). Regularized control supplies the Gibbs policy and the geometry of the value gap (Geist et al., 2019; O’Donoghue, 2022). The relation between policy gradients and soft Q-learning provides another view of these coordinates (Schulman et al., 2017). DPO and its sequential extension relate language-model policies to rewards and action values during post-training (Rafailov et al., 2023; Rafailov et al., 2024).

Our optimal action score combines the optimal semantic action value with the semantic reference prior. These coordinates let us compare the decisions induced by different interfaces and measure a deployed policy’s gap to each optimum. The analysis of fine-tuning objectives by Swamy et al. (2025) likewise uses a common geometric description to distinguish ideal equivalence from differences that emerge in practice. Here the distinction concerns the interface’s optimal decisions and the choices that a particular checkpoint makes through it.

Behavioral identification and reward transfer. Inverse RL recovers rewards from behavior subject to ambiguities (Ng and Russell, 2000; Russell, 1998). Reward shaping using a potential function preserves optimal policies (Ng et al., 1999). Analyses of identifiability under entropy regularization and of partial identifiability characterize the corresponding reward classes (Cao et al., 2021; Skalse et al., 2023). EPIC compares reward functions while accounting for transformations that preserve policies (Gleave et al., 2021). Work on the transferability of rewards recovered through regularized inverse RL further studies changes in transition laws (Schlaginhaufen and Kamgarpour, 2024).

Our equivalence class for a single interface removes statewise constants from the scores. Appendix C distinguishes this behavioral object from the nonunique decomposition into prior, reward, and transition. The transfer analysis then compares the target energy with the actual deployed readout, weighting their discrepancy by deployment occupancy.

Interface and agent design. Interface design and prompt formatting affect agent behavior (Yang et al., 2024; Sclar et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a). GUI-360∘ reports higher action prediction accuracy for GPT-4o and lower accuracy for fine-tuned Qwen after adding accessibility metadata and replacing coordinate arguments with element IDs (Mu et al., 2025). ADAS and AFlow search over agent implementations and workflows (Hu et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). Darwin Gödel Machine and Self-Improving Coding Agent revise scaffolds and assess them through execution (Zhang et al., 2026; Robeyns et al., 2025). Promptbreeder, ToolMaker, and MAS-ZERO respectively explore prompts, tools, and designs involving multiple agents (Fernando et al., 2023; Wölflein et al., 2025; Ke et al., 2025). Surveys place these approaches within agent systems with mechanisms for self improvement (Fang et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026).

These design procedures can change action opportunities, realizations, or both. Our analysis separates each candidate’s optimal return from the evaluated checkpoint’s gap to that optimum. This distinction connects execution feedback to two possible sources of improvement: a more useful decision problem and a policy that better realizes its available decisions.

Context and harness distillation. Context distillation trains a model to reproduce, without the prompt, the behavior that the prompt elicits (Snell et al., 2022). Harness-Zero distills a specialized harness into the weights by letting a harnessing agent correct the student’s responses in the target harness’s action space (Ye et al., 2026). Our identification result states which decision information such training can carry, the relative action scores of the training harness. The readout study shows that the learned preferences are still expressed through the deployment interface, so a distilled policy can change its choices when the interface changes.

Joint adaptation of harnesses and model weights. Joint adaptation takes several forms: SIA selects harness and weight updates, Co-Harness trains from trajectories collected under revised interfaces, and WHALE alternates training with harness search (Hebbar et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2026). Yu et al. (2026) find that imitating expert trajectories can hurt a weaker model under an evolved harness while on-policy correction helps, and HarnessBandit schedules training across harnesses by learnability and transferability (Wei et al., 2026).

These methods can use the ceiling and the mismatch to tell whether a candidate harness offers too little or is not yet used well. Our adaptation threshold specifies the mismatch reduction needed to make a revision with a higher ceiling beneficial. Eq. (24) isolates how a weight update changes a revision’s relative value. Comparisons across checkpoints and interfaces therefore track both recovery after a revision and changes in interface rankings. The controlled protocol measures this interaction separately from gains under either interface alone.

Appendix B Semantic Control: Objects, Abstraction, and Objectives

B.1 Notation and Standing Conditions

The formal results use finite state and action spaces, bounded rewards, 0≤γ<10\leq\gamma<1, τ>0\tau>0, and a reference prior that is positive on every available action. The initial distribution, reward units, and regularization coefficient are shared in a comparison across interfaces. State/action alignments are fixed before the comparison. Results involving log⁡Πθ,ℐ\log\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}} additionally require positive probabilities for the actual policy on the probed actions. The gap identity for a fixed interface itself allows zero policy probabilities, with 0​log⁡0=00\log 0=0.

We use a reference checkpoint distinct from the evolving evaluated checkpoint. When its sequence distribution is πref\pi_{\rm ref}, a natural semantic reference is

πℐref(a∣s)=∑y:dℐ​(y,s)=aπref(y∣cℐ(s)).\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}}(a\mid s)=\sum_{y:d_{\mathcal{I}}(y;s)=a}\pi_{\rm ref}(y\mid c_{\mathcal{I}}(s)). (13)

Consequently a new encoding can change both the target induced by the reference and the evaluated model’s readout. Experiments that hold the target fixed must verify or explicitly control this reference.

B.2 Decision Epochs and Controller State

A semantic state includes every variable needed to predict the state at the next decision: the task state, visible history or a sufficient summary, tool results, budget counters, and controller memory. An action denotes a fully specified operation, such as invoking a particular tool with particular arguments, or submitting a particular candidate. Two output strings belong to one semantic action only when the decoder and executor execute the same operation at that state.

After a semantic action is selected, eℐe_{\mathcal{I}} can execute a fixed tool, perform a deterministic check, or apply a stochastic transition independent of the policy. Its expected costs enter rℐr_{\mathcal{I}}, and its outcomes enter PℐP_{\mathcal{I}}. If a retry, verifier, or stopping rule calls the evaluated model for another decision, that call is another decision epoch in the expanded state space. This keeps the transition kernel fixed while the policy varies.

An invalid string is mapped to an explicit failure or recovery action. Similarly, when an empirical action vocabulary groups outputs into an “other” category, that category must have a defined execution interpretation. Discarding unmodeled outputs changes the policy being measured.

B.3 When Training over Tokens Induces Semantic Optimality

Let Ya​(s)Y_{a}(s) be the set of complete output realizations decoded as action aa. Write a sequence policy and reference as

p⁡(y∣s)=pA​(a∣s)​p​(y∣s,a),ρ⁡(y∣s)=ρA​(a∣s)​ρ​(y∣s,a),y∈Ya​(s).p(y\mid s)=p_{A}(a\mid s)p(y\mid s,a),\qquad\rho(y\mid s)=\rho_{A}(a\mid s)\rho(y\mid s,a),\quad y\in Y_{a}(s).

For any such distributions, the KL chain rule gives

KL(p(⋅∣s)∥ρ(⋅∣s))=KL(pA(⋅∣s)∥ρA(⋅∣s))+𝔼a∼pAKL(p(⋅∣s,a)∥ρ(⋅∣s,a)).\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot\mid s)\|\rho(\cdot\mid s))=\mathrm{KL}(p_{A}(\cdot\mid s)\|\rho_{A}(\cdot\mid s))+\mathbb{E}_{a\sim p_{A}}\mathrm{KL}(p(\cdot\mid s,a)\|\rho(\cdot\mid s,a)). (14)

Suppose reward, transition, and discount are identical within each fiber. Then the return from choosing yy depends only on aa, while the second term in Eq. (14) is minimized by retaining the reference conditional distribution inside that fiber. Optimization over complete sequence actions therefore reduces exactly to the semantic control problem regularized by KL divergence relative to ρA\rho_{A}.

For an autoregressive model, probabilities of complete sequences include termination. The expected sum of token KL divergences equals sequence KL when the same terminating sequence measure and matching token conditionals are used. Rewards that depend on tokens, discounts that depend on sequence length, or additional model decisions within a proposed temporally extended action require the expanded model above.

Appendix C Behavioral Identification and Mechanism Ambiguity

C.1 Soft Bellman Optimality

For a fixed interface, the optimal Bellman operator is

(𝒯​V)​(s)=τ​log​∑aπref​(a∣s)​exp⁡(r(s,a)+γ𝔼P(⋅∣s,a)V(s′)τ).(\mathcal{T}V)(s)=\tau\log\sum_{a}\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid s)\exp\left(\frac{r(s,a)+\gamma\mathbb{E}_{P(\cdot\mid s,a)}V(s^{\prime})}{\tau}\right).

Monotonicity of the log partition function and its translation identity imply ‖𝒯​V−𝒯​W‖∞≤γ​‖V−W‖∞\left\lVert\mathcal{T}V-\mathcal{T}W\right\rVert_{\infty}\leq\gamma\left\lVert V-W\right\rVert_{\infty}. Thus it has a unique fixed point V∗V^{*}, and Q∗=r+γ​P​V∗Q^{*}=r+\gamma PV^{*} is uniquely determined. At each state, maximizing ∑aπa​Qa∗−τ​∑aπa​log⁡(πa/ρa)\sum_{a}\pi_{a}Q_{a}^{*}-\tau\sum_{a}\pi_{a}\log(\pi_{a}/\rho_{a}) over the simplex gives

πa∗=ρa​eQa∗/τ∑bρb​eQb∗/τ.\pi_{a}^{*}=\frac{\rho_{a}e^{Q_{a}^{*}/\tau}}{\sum_{b}\rho_{b}e^{Q_{b}^{*}/\tau}}.

Strict concavity gives uniqueness. At the fixed point, V∗​(s)=τ​log​∑bρb​eQb∗/τV^{*}(s)=\tau\log\sum_{b}\rho_{b}e^{Q_{b}^{*}/\tau}, so the optimal policy takes the Gibbs form

Π∗​(a∣s)=πref​(a∣s)​exp⁡(Q∗​(s,a)−V∗​(s)τ).\Pi^{*}(a\mid s)=\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}(a\mid s)\exp\!\left(\frac{Q^{*}(s,a)-V^{*}(s)}{\tau}\right). (15)

Substituting Fa∗=Qa∗+τ​log⁡ρaF_{a}^{*}=Q_{a}^{*}+\tau\log\rho_{a} produces the softmax representation in the main text.

C.2 Proof of Proposition 3.1

If F⁡(s,⋅)=G⁡(s,⋅)+c⁡(s)​𝟏F(s,\cdot)=G(s,\cdot)+c(s)\mathbf{1}, the factor ec⁡(s)/τe^{c(s)/\tau} cancels in softmax. Conversely, equal softmax probabilities imply

F⁡(s,a)−Φ⁡(F⁡(s,⋅))=G⁡(s,a)−Φ⁡(G⁡(s,⋅))F(s,a)-\Phi(F(s,\cdot))=G(s,a)-\Phi(G(s,\cdot))

for every action. Their difference is therefore constant across actions. Applying this equivalence to optimal action scores proves the first assertion. Under Πθ,ℐtr=Πℐtr∗\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}=\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}, the Gibbs identity gives

τ​log⁡Πθ,ℐtr​(a∣s)=Fℐtr∗​(s,a)−Vℐtr∗​(s).\tau\log\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}(a\mid s)=F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}(s,a)-V^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{\rm tr}}(s).

C.3 Mechanism Nonidentifiability

Proposition C.1 (Mechanism nonidentifiability).

A fixed optimal score field can be realized by a continuous family of different reference priors and rewards, and even by different transition laws. Consequently, optimal behavior alone does not uniquely determine the interface mechanism.

Proof.

Fix a finite score field FF, any reference ρ′\rho^{\prime} with full support, and any stochastic kernel P′P^{\prime}. Define

V⁡(s)=Φ⁡(F⁡(s,⋅)),Q′​(s,a)=F⁡(s,a)−τ​log​ρ′​(a∣s),r′=Q′−γ​P′​V.V(s)=\Phi(F(s,\cdot)),\qquad Q^{\prime}(s,a)=F(s,a)-\tau\log\rho^{\prime}(a\mid s),\qquad r^{\prime}=Q^{\prime}-\gamma P^{\prime}V.

Then Q′=r′+γ​P′​VQ^{\prime}=r^{\prime}+\gamma P^{\prime}V, and

τ​log​∑aρ′​(a∣s)​eQ′​(s,a)/τ=τ​log​∑aeF⁡(s,a)/τ=V⁡(s).\tau\log\sum_{a}\rho^{\prime}(a\mid s)e^{Q^{\prime}(s,a)/\tau}=\tau\log\sum_{a}e^{F(s,a)/\tau}=V(s).

By uniqueness of the Bellman fixed point, these are the optimal values of the constructed control problem. Its optimal policy is softmax⁡(F/τ)\operatorname{softmax}(F/\tau). Varying ρ′\rho^{\prime} or P′P^{\prime} gives a continuous family of mechanisms with the same scores and policy. ∎
