D.5 A Two-Action Illustration of Reversal and Adaptation

Consider a bandit with two actions and a uniform reference. The source execution protocol gives rewards (1,0)(1,0), and its optimal policy chooses the first action with probability p=e1/τ/(1+e1/τ)p=e^{1/\tau}/(1+e^{1/\tau}). A revised protocol lowers the first action’s utility to 00 and raises the second action’s utility to u>0u>0. Holding the semantic policy fixed isolates the effect of this change in action values.

The two ceilings are

C1=τ​log⁡e1/τ+12,C2=τ​log⁡1+eu/τ2.C_{1}=\tau\log\frac{e^{1/\tau}+1}{2},\qquad C_{2}=\tau\log\frac{1+e^{u/\tau}}{2}.

Hence C2>C1C_{2}>C_{1} if and only if u>1u>1. Holding the actual policy fixed also holds its reference KL fixed. Its returns satisfy

J2−J1=u⁡(1−p)−p.J_{2}-J_{1}=u(1-p)-p.

The policy gains uu when it takes the second action and loses 11 when it takes the first. Its return therefore improves only when u>p/(1−p)=e1/τu>p/(1-p)=e^{1/\tau}. Throughout 1<u<e1/τ1<u<e^{1/\tau}, the revised interface has a higher ceiling and a lower deployed return: the unchanged policy still favors the action preferred under the source optimum.

Because the source policy is optimal, Corollary 5.2 makes the revision beneficial once the remaining mismatch is smaller than C2−C1C_{2}-C_{1}. Reaching the new optimum realizes this entire gain, positive for every u>1u>1. Figure 7 plots the frozen policy’s return change and the ceiling gain at τ=0.5\tau=0.5, with the vertical distance between the curves giving the mismatch under the revised interface. All quantities here are analytical.

D.6 Policy Adaptation and Interface Rankings

Proof of Corollary 5.2.

Keep the evaluation objective and reference fixed for each interface. Substituting J⁡(θ,ℐj)=Cj−M⁡(θ,ℐj)J(\theta,\mathcal{I}_{j})=C_{j}-M(\theta,\mathcal{I}_{j}) gives

J⁡(θ0,ℐ2)−J⁡(θ0,ℐ1)\displaystyle J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{2})-J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}) =Δ​C+M⁡(θ0,ℐ1)−M⁡(θ0,ℐ2),\displaystyle=\Delta C+M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1})-M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{2}),
J⁡(θ1,ℐ2)−J⁡(θ0,ℐ1)\displaystyle J(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2})-J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}) =Δ​C+M⁡(θ0,ℐ1)−M⁡(θ1,ℐ2).\displaystyle=\Delta C+M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1})-M(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2}).

The initially harmful revision makes the first difference negative. Since Δ​C+M⁡(θ0,ℐ1)=C2−J⁡(θ0,ℐ1)\Delta C+M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1})=C_{2}-J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}), the second is positive exactly under Eq. (10). Combining the initial harm and subsequent improvement gives the equivalent chain

M⁡(θ1,ℐ2)<Δ​C+M⁡(θ0,ℐ1)<M⁡(θ0,ℐ2).M(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{2})<\Delta C+M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1})<M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{2}).

The source pair’s mismatch M⁡(θ0,ℐ1)M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}) allows for a source checkpoint that has not reached its optimum. For an optimal source policy, the threshold equals the ceiling gain Δ​C\Delta C, and reaching the new optimum realizes the entire gain. ∎

Interaction between weight and interface updates.

For j∈{1,2}j\in\{1,2\}, define the gain from the weight update in interface jj by

Aj=J⁡(θ1,ℐj)−J⁡(θ0,ℐj)=M⁡(θ0,ℐj)−M⁡(θ1,ℐj).A_{j}=J(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{j})-J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{j})=M(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{j})-M(\theta_{1},\mathcal{I}_{j}).

Write Δ​J​(θ)=J⁡(θ,ℐ2)−J⁡(θ,ℐ1)\Delta J(\theta)=J(\theta,\mathcal{I}_{2})-J(\theta,\mathcal{I}_{1}) for the relative value of the revision. The interaction across the four combinations is

Ω=Δ​J​(θ1)−Δ​J​(θ0)=A2−A1.\Omega=\Delta J(\theta_{1})-\Delta J(\theta_{0})=A_{2}-A_{1}. (24)

The ceiling terms cancel because the objectives are fixed across checkpoints. A positive Ω\Omega means the revision becomes relatively more valuable after the weight update. If Δ​J​(θ0)<0\Delta J(\theta_{0})<0, its ranking reverses exactly when Ω>−Δ​J​(θ0)\Omega>-\Delta J(\theta_{0}). This compares the two interfaces at the updated checkpoint, while Corollary 5.2 compares the adapted pair with the source pair. Reporting A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} also identifies the source of the interaction: deterioration under the source interface (A1<0A_{1}<0) can increase Ω\Omega even when A2=0A_{2}=0.

Appendix E Measurement Theory

E.1 Curvature on the Decision Quotient

For p=softmax⁡(F/τ)p=\operatorname{softmax}(F/\tau),

∇2Φ​(F)=1τ​(diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤).\nabla^{2}\Phi(F)=\frac{1}{\tau}\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}\bigr). (25)

The categorical covariance annihilates 𝟏\mathbf{1}. Its spectral norm is at most 1/21/2: the absolute row sum of row ii is 2​pi​(1−pi)≤1/22p_{i}(1-p_{i})\leq 1/2, and the matrix is symmetric. If pi≥pminp_{i}\geq p_{\min} and z⟂𝟏z\perp\mathbf{1}, then

z⊤​(diag⁡(p)−p​p⊤)​z\displaystyle z^{\top}\bigl(\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^{\top}\bigr)z =min⁡∑ic⁡pi​(zi−c)2\displaystyle=\min_{c}\sum_{i}p_{i}(z_{i}-c)^{2}
≥pmin​min⁡∑ic⁡(zi−c)2=pmin​‖z‖22.\displaystyle\geq p_{\min}\min_{c}\sum_{i}(z_{i}-c)^{2}=p_{\min}\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Thus the upper Hessian constant is 1/(2​τ)1/(2\tau) and the lower constant on the centered subspace is pmin/τp_{\min}/\tau.

E.2 Bounds on the Performance Gap

Proposition 6.1 bounds mismatch through centered score error. An upper bound below the threshold in Corollary 5.2 guarantees recovery of the source pair’s return. Under a condition on probability overlap, the same score error also provides a lower bound on mismatch. We state the complementary bound and prove both results below.

Corollary E.1 (Complementary lower bound).

With xsx_{s} and εd\varepsilon_{d} as in Proposition 6.1, let pmin>0p_{\min}>0 be a uniform lower bound on action probabilities along the score interpolation between the actual and optimal policies. Then

pmin​εd22​τ​(1−γ)≤M⁡(θ,ℐ)≤εd24​τ​(1−γ).\frac{p_{\min}\varepsilon_{d}^{2}}{2\tau(1-\gamma)}\leq M(\theta,\mathcal{I})\leq\frac{\varepsilon_{d}^{2}}{4\tau(1-\gamma)}. (26)

Proof of both bounds.

At a fixed state, let x=F^−F¯∗x=\widehat{F}-\bar{F}^{*}, with both arguments centered. Taylor’s integral remainder gives

DΦ​(F¯∗,F^)=∫01(1−t)​x⊤​∇2Φ​(F^+t⁡(F¯∗−F^))​x​𝑑t.D_{\Phi}(\bar{F}^{*},\widehat{F})=\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)x^{\top}\nabla^{2}\Phi\bigl(\widehat{F}+t(\bar{F}^{*}-\widehat{F})\bigr)x\,\mathrm{d}t.

The curvature bounds above and ∫01(1−t)​𝑑t=1/2\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\,\mathrm{d}t=1/2 imply

pmin2​τ​‖x‖22≤DΦ​(F¯∗,F^)≤14​τ​‖x‖22.\frac{p_{\min}}{2\tau}\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}^{2}\leq D_{\Phi}(\bar{F}^{*},\widehat{F})\leq\frac{1}{4\tau}\left\lVert x\right\rVert_{2}^{2}.

Taking the actual occupancy expectation and dividing by 1−γ1-\gamma proves both bounds. ∎

A lower probability bound at both endpoint policies is sufficient along their score interpolation: the logarithm of softmax is concave in the score vector, so each interpolated log probability is at least the linear interpolation of its endpoint log probabilities.

The quadratic upper rate and constant are locally tight. For two actions around the uniform distribution, the categorical covariance has eigenvalue 1/21/2 on 𝟏⟂\mathbf{1}^{\perp}, so DΦ​(F,F+z)=‖z‖22/(4​τ)+o⁡(‖z‖22)D_{\Phi}(F,F+z)=\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}/(4\tau)+o(\left\lVert z\right\rVert_{2}^{2}) for centered zz. No positive quadratic lower constant independent of the action probabilities is possible: near a policy concentrated on one action, the nonconstant curvature can approach zero.

Appendix F Experimental Details

We describe the experiments in the order of the main text: the MiniWoB++ setup and post-training study, the readout study, the H0-to-H1 adaptation study, the adaptation across harness swaps, the calibration of finite measurements, the independent prediction study, the coding-agent harness study, and the exact comparison of harness scores with task success.

F.1 MiniWoB++ Setup and Post-Training

The controlled study pairs language-model post-training with a finite control model of each harness. This gives every checkpoint a fixed optimal policy to compare against, while retaining task instructions, parameterized actions, and controller feedback in the model’s input.

We compare six harnesses, H0–H5, using H0 as the direct baseline.

Tasks and observations.

We use three tasks from MiniWoB++ (Liu et al., 2018). In click-checkboxes, the agent toggles checkboxes to match the requested labels and submits the selection. In click-checkboxes-soft, the requested words and checkbox labels are matched by synonym meaning. In ascending-numbers, the agent clicks five tiles in numerical order, with the remaining numbers hidden after the first click. We retain the initially visible layout in the public observation, together with spatial tile IDs, the remaining tiles, and the number of completed clicks. Checkbox observations contain the instruction, each label and its checked status. All actor observations also expose the remaining decision budget and the harness’s controller state.

The reward is one for exact task completion and zero otherwise, including partial completion. All explicit action and tool costs are zero. Each episode allows at most ten actor decisions, with discount γ=0.95\gamma=0.95 per decision. We compile the physical transitions, remaining budget, and controller memory into a finite acyclic graph. For every retained task, we verify a successful run in the native browser and separately compare the compiled transitions and termination rules with the page behavior. Training and exhaustive policy evaluation use these compiled graphs.

Harnesses.

Table 4 specifies the six interfaces. The program verifier approves an action when it avoids an incorrect terminal outcome, using the public instruction, page state, and the benchmark’s fixed synonym vocabulary. Verification targets are checkbox submission and each of the five tile clicks. H4 uses a separate frozen Qwen3.5-2B reviewer whose prompt contains the public task and physical page state together with the proposed action, omitting the actor’s remaining budget and controller memory. It greedily selects between single-token approve/reject codes. For H3 and H4, verification feedback becomes part of the next observation and is cleared by a native action. The H1 batch executes two ordered clicks within one actor decision and stops at native termination, so it receives only one discount step. All ordered pairs of click IDs are available, including repeated IDs.

Data splits.

We generate tasks with the native pages and deduplicate them by full public task content before assigning splits. Table 5 gives the fixed counts. Checkbox instances contain fewer than five boxes, and in the number task the first required number lies in one of the first three spatial positions. The 72-task training probe is fixed before training and is a subset of the training set. The six harnesses share the same task contents and splits. Test tasks are held out from parameter updates.

All MiniWoB++ experiments reported in this paper use the same fixed test set of 576 tasks generated from MiniWoB++, with 192 tasks per family. Calibration and training-probe tasks remain separate.

Policy readout and reference.

The actor receives a system message specifying the task and harness rules and a JSON observation listing every available action. Each complete action, including its arguments, maps bijectively to one case-sensitive token from A--Z/a--z. We normalize the next-token logits over this full menu at sampling temperature one, using the model’s chat template with thinking disabled. This categorical distribution defines Πθ,ℐh\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{h}} throughout training and evaluation. The base model and tokenizer are Qwen3.5-2B. An independent frozen copy, without the trained adapter, reads the same messages to define πℐhref\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}_{h}} at each state. The reference stays fixed across checkpoints. Because H5 changes the reference model’s input as well as the actor’s, we solve its regularized optimum separately from H0’s even though their execution dynamics coincide.

Training distribution and objective.

Each harness starts from the same base weights and initial LoRA adapter (Hu et al., 2022). To retain correction states as successful behavior becomes more frequent, training uses

μh=12​δs0,h+12​νh,Jμh​(θ)=𝔼μh,Πθ,ℐh,Ph​∑t≥0γt​[rh​(st,at)−τ​log⁡Πθ,ℐh​(at∣st)πℐhref​(at∣st)],\mu_{h}=\tfrac{1}{2}\delta_{s_{0,h}}+\tfrac{1}{2}\nu_{h},\qquad J_{\mu_{h}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mu_{h},\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{h}},P_{h}}\sum_{t\geq 0}\gamma^{t}\left[r_{h}(s_{t},a_{t})-\tau\log\frac{\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{h}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}{\pi^{\mathrm{ref}}_{\mathcal{I}_{h}}(a_{t}\mid s_{t})}\right], (27)

with τ=0.1\tau=0.1. Here s0,hs_{0,h} is the native task start. We form νh\nu_{h} from all other reachable nonterminal states, stratifying by correction category or completion progress, remaining-budget bin, and controller memory. Checkbox categories are correct, missing selections only, extra selections only, and both missing and extra selections. For the number task, categories are defined by the number of completed clicks. Budget bins are 1–3, 4–6, and 7–9 remaining decisions. We assign equal mass to nonempty strata and then to states within each stratum. Each start has a legal action prefix from the native state, and the objective begins at that start with its remaining budget. This gives every reachable decision state positive training mass while leaving the statewise dynamics, rewards, and optimal action preferences fixed.

Exact-PG updates.

Each update samples four tasks with replacement, first choosing a task family uniformly and then an instance uniformly within that family. For each task, dynamic programming evaluates the current policy’s regularized value and advantage, and propagates discounted visitation from μh\mu_{h}. Exact-PG sums the policy gradient over this task’s reachable states and complete action menu. Gradients for the four tasks are evaluated at the same parameters and averaged once per optimizer step. The objective thus weights tasks equally regardless of graph size. A separate soft Bellman solve provides Πℐh∗\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{h}} and Fℐh∗F^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{h}} as evaluation targets. Table 6 gives the optimization settings.

Each training run uses one RTX 4090 GPU.

Geometry and return measurements.

At initialization and each saved checkpoint, we read the complete action distribution at every reachable nonterminal state of all calibration and training-probe tasks. For a task uu, let 𝒮h,u\mathcal{S}_{h,u} denote this fixed state bank. Its geometry error is

MSEh,u⁡(θ)=1|𝒮h,u|​∑s∈𝒮h,u‖τP⟂[logΠθ,ℐh(⋅∣s)−logΠ∗ℐh(⋅∣s)]‖22|𝒜h,u​(s)|.\operatorname{MSE}_{h,u}(\theta)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{S}_{h,u}|}\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{h,u}}\frac{\left\lVert\tau P_{\!\perp}\!\left[\log\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{h}}(\cdot\mid s)-\log\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{h}}(\cdot\mid s)\right]\right\rVert_{2}^{2}}{|\mathcal{A}_{h,u}(s)|}. (28)

We average this quantity within task families and then across the three families. The fixed bank makes the trajectory of this error comparable across checkpoints, including decisions that become rare under the learned policy. Alongside it, we compute native-start success probability, JJ, CC, and the squared score error weighted by the evaluated policy’s discounted occupancy. Success is the undiscounted probability of exact completion, evaluated by dynamic programming. Mismatch is computed independently as τ/(1−γ)\tau/(1-\gamma) times the occupancy-weighted KL(Πθ,ℐh∥Πℐh∗)\mathrm{KL}(\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}_{h}}\|\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{h}}), allowing comparison with C−JC-J. We sum over nonterminal states without renormalizing their occupancy mass.

Transfer and uncertainty.

For transfer, we evaluate the six trained actors at the common final update 1,024 under all six deployment harnesses on the fixed test set, which gives the 6×66\times 6 matrix in Figure 3. Every cell uses its deployment harness’s state graph, menu, frozen reference, and optimal target. Comparisons within a column therefore hold the deployment control problem fixed.

The learning curves in Figure 3 use all 288 calibration tasks at initialization and every 64 updates through update 1,024. For both success and geometry MSE, we form pointwise 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 bootstrap resamples of tasks within each family. The same task draws are shared across metrics and checkpoints, with equal weight on each family. Changes from initialization use paired differences under these same draws. All measured checkpoints are plotted without smoothing. We make the same measurements on the 72-task training probe. From initialization to update 1,024, the geometry error falls by 69% to 90% across the six harnesses, both on the training probe and on the calibration tasks, which play no role in parameter updates. For each harness, the two reductions differ by less than one percentage point. Post-training thus improves the geometry on held-out and training tasks alike.

F.2 Readout Study

Tasks and frozen checkpoint.

The main-text comparison uses the H0-trained Qwen3.5-2B checkpoint at post-training update 1,024. Its weights remain frozen throughout evaluation. We evaluate it on the fixed test set in Table 5, the same 576 tasks used by the adaptation and prediction studies below. R0 therefore reproduces the source checkpoint’s H0 results in Table 8.

Presentation variants.

R0 uses the canonical H0 system message, JSON observation, and action-code mapping. R1 reverses the order of top-level observation fields while preserving their contents and the nested action dictionary. R2 replaces the action dictionary with a list of records containing the same code and action fields. R3 shifts the action-code assignment cyclically by one position, R4 reverses it, and R5 uses a fixed random permutation for each menu size. These three variants preserve the order and full arguments of the semantic actions and update the displayed code assignment and decoder together. We align every probability table by semantic action before comparison. The system message and all task information are unchanged, and inputs are evaluated without truncation.

Shared reference and exact evaluation.

We fix the semantic reference q0​(a∣s)q_{0}(a\mid s) to the frozen base model’s distribution under R0 and assign this same probability to the corresponding code in each variant. The evaluated actor reads each variant normally. All conditions use H0’s native actions and dynamics, ten model decisions, γ=0.95\gamma=0.95, τ=0.1\tau=0.1, and zero explicit costs. The full legal single-token menu is evaluated at sampling temperature one. Model forward passes use BF16 with state microbatches of eight, followed by FP64 probability normalization and control calculations. We enumerate reachable states, solve the optimum separately in each code ordering, and compute return and success from the measured semantic policy by dynamic programming. Mismatch is computed independently from occupancy-weighted KL(Π∥Π∗)\mathrm{KL}(\Pi\|\Pi^{*}). The largest ceiling difference is 2.2×10−162.2\times 10^{-16} and the largest optimal-action probability difference is 8.3×10−168.3\times 10^{-16} across variants.

Measurements and uncertainty.

Choice change is the fraction of states where the most probable semantic action differs from R0. Readout RMS is the square root of the mean squared entries of η=τ​P⟂​(log⁡Πθ,Rv−log⁡Πθ,R0)\eta=\tau P_{\!\perp}(\log\Pi_{\theta,R_{v}}-\log\Pi_{\theta,R_{0}}). We average state-level measurements within each task, then average tasks within each family and give the three families equal weight. All variants are evaluated on the same tasks. We form percentile intervals from 2,000 paired task bootstrap resamples within families. These intervals quantify task variation at the fixed checkpoint. Table 7 reports the readout and performance measurements.

F.3 Adaptation After an Interface Revision

Revision and source checkpoint.

We study H0-to-H1 adaptation using the model, task families, action decoder, and harness definitions of Appendix F.1. H1 retains H0’s native actions and adds ordered pairs of clicks executed within one actor decision, stopping at native termination. The source checkpoint θ0\theta_{0} is the H0-trained Qwen3.5-2B model at post-training update 1,024.

Tasks and splits.

Training reuses the 1,440 training tasks and the coverage mixture μh\mu_{h} in Eq. (27). The evaluation reuses all 576 tasks in Table 5, with 192 instances per family. These tasks are held out from parameter updates and checkpoint selection. We reuse the same task graphs, action menus, and reference probabilities as the post-training study. All deployment metrics start from the native task starts ρ0\rho_{0}.

Training branches and budget.

Both branches inherit the same source LoRA weights and reset AdamW’s first and second moments. One continues under H0, giving θs\theta_{s}, and the other adapts under H1, giving θt\theta_{t}. Both use paired task draws. Each receives 1,024 additional Exact-PG updates with four tasks per update, for 4,096 task draws. We retain the post-training settings in Table 6, including LoRA rank 16 and scale 32, constant learning rate 10−510^{-5}, BF16 forward passes, and state microbatches of eight. Each interface’s dynamics, costs, frozen base-model reference, γ=0.95\gamma=0.95, and τ=0.1\tau=0.1 stay fixed throughout training and evaluation.

Evaluation schedule and measurements.

We evaluate at additional updates 0, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, and 1,024. The source checkpoint is evaluated under both interfaces, and each later checkpoint from both branches is evaluated under both interfaces, giving 26 complete evaluations. The budget and checkpoint schedule were fixed before adaptation. The endpoint comparisons use update 1,024, and the curves include every scheduled checkpoint.

The oracle solves the soft Bellman equations for CjC_{j} and Πℐj∗\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}_{j}}. Complete action probabilities and the evaluated policy’s forward discounted visitation determine MM through Eq. (6). Terminal states contribute zero loss, and nonterminal visitation mass is retained without renormalization. Independently, Bellman policy evaluation computes JJ, while undiscounted policy evaluation gives task success. The residual in J=C−MJ=C-M checks numerical consistency. These measurements use the compiled task graphs and full action distributions.

Comparisons.

For each branch, we compare the target-interface mismatch with the fixed recovery threshold C2−J⁡(θ0,ℐ1)C_{2}-J(\theta_{0},\mathcal{I}_{1}). We separately evaluate recovery beyond the source pair, interface ranking for the updated checkpoint, and the return difference between the H1-adapted pair and continued training under H0. Evaluating both branches under H1 also measures the effect of the training interface at a common deployment interface. We report the component gains A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} and their difference Ω\Omega from Appendix D.6, alongside regularized return and task success.

Uncertainty and computation.

Metrics average tasks within each family and weight the families equally. We form pointwise 95% percentile intervals from 2,000 paired bootstrap resamples within families. The same resampling indices are shared across checkpoints, interfaces, metrics, and paired differences. Each branch trains on one RTX 4090 GPU, and a third GPU evaluates checkpoints.

Adaptation results.

H1 has a higher ceiling than H0, and both stay fixed across checkpoints. The frozen swap increases mismatch enough to outweigh this gain and lower return. H1 adaptation then reduces mismatch below the recovery threshold, and the final adapted pair exceeds both the source H0 pair and H0 continuation under H0. Table 8 gives the measurements of the source checkpoint and both final checkpoints. Rising return under H1 and falling return under H0 together reverse the ranking along the adaptation branch.

The interface ranking reverses before the adapted pair recovers the source pair’s return. At the first recorded checkpoint with a positive mean recovery difference, its paired interval still includes zero. By the final budget, the paired intervals for recovery and improvement over H0 continuation both lie above zero. Table 9 reports these endpoint comparisons, and Figure 5 shows the recovery and ranking trajectories. In the notation of Appendix D.6, ℐ1\mathcal{I}_{1} is H0 and ℐ2\mathcal{I}_{2} is H1.

F.4 Adaptation Across Harness Swaps

Among the 30 ordered swaps between H0–H5, a frozen comparison rejects 22, and 13 of those have T≤0T\leq 0, which leaves nine. Each of the nine starts from the checkpoint post-trained under its source harness in Appendix F.1 and adapts under the target harness with the protocol of Appendix F.3. We recorded the predictions for the eight swaps other than H0→\toH1 before adapting them.

Table 10 lists the nine swaps. For the eight swaps recorded in advance, T−r2T-r_{2} orders the gains with Spearman ρ=0.95\rho=0.95, the ceiling gain alone with ρ=0.86\rho=0.86, and the frozen return change with ρ=0.17\rho=0.17. Subtracting the frozen return change and the gain from TT gives the target mismatch before and after adaptation. It falls from between 0.015 and 0.146 to at most 0.019. The observed gain exceeds T−r2T-r_{2} in every swap, by 0.004 on average. The ranking predicted from the checkpoint post-trained under the target has the correct sign in all eight recorded swaps and orders the observed rankings with Spearman ρ=0.91\rho=0.91. After adapting from H1 to H0, the checkpoint prefers H0 by 0.041 and still falls short of the source pair, so a ranking reversal alone does not show a net gain. Adapting from H0 to H5 also beats continued training under H0 by 0.085​[0.078, 0.092]0.085\ [0.078,\,0.092]. The 13 swaps with T≤0T\leq 0 include all five swaps from H5, with TT between −0.136-0.136 and −0.016-0.016.

F.5 Calibration of Finite Mismatch Measurements

Estimator.

For each task and deployed pair, draw mm independent pilot trajectories. For each trajectory, draw TT with Pr⁡(T=t)=(1−γ)​γt\Pr(T=t)=(1-\gamma)\gamma^{t} and retain its state sTs_{T}. Retaining one state per independent trajectory gives independent occupancy samples. A draw after termination contributes zero to the average over all mm draws. At each nonterminal sampled state with KK actions, draw NN independent actions and form

p~​(a∣s)=na+αN+K​α.\widetilde{p}(a\mid s)=\frac{n_{a}+\alpha}{N+K\alpha}. (29)

These smoothed distributions enter the mismatch estimate in Eq. (11). Each nonterminal state draw uses the complete deployed action menu. Pilot and action-sampling queries are both counted.

Candidate budgets and smoothing.

The grid uses m∈{64,256}m\in\{64,256\} and N∈{16,64,256,1024}N\in\{16,64,256,1024\}. Four smoothing rules use a pseudocount of 0.10.1 or 0.50.5 per action, or a total pseudocount β∈{0.5,1}\beta\in\{0.5,1\} divided across the KK actions. This gives 32 candidates. Calibration uses 32 independent measurement pools, with shared nested prefixes across candidates. For each candidate, the calibration scorer computes the expected absolute-mismatch bias using exact occupancy and the binomial marginal distribution of each action count. The predictor receives only the sampled observations.

Selection criteria.

A candidate must meet three criteria over H0 and H1 at every adaptation node: absolute expected mismatch bias at most 0.0050.005 averaged over families, bias at most 0.010.01 within every family, and aggregate return-difference RMSE at most 0.010.01 for recovery and ranking across measurement pools. It must also reach RMSE at most 0.030.03 on the configuration calibration set. Among passing candidates, we select the lowest mean realized actor-query cost. Costs within 1% tie and are resolved by worst-node difference RMSE, mm, NN, and the fixed smoothing-rule order.

Four candidates pass, all with m=256m=256 and N=1024N=1024. The selected rule uses α=0.5\alpha=0.5 per action and has configuration calibration RMSE 0.008870.00887. Each test prediction uses a single measurement pool. Table 11 compares the initial and selected budgets, and Figure 8 shows the full sweep.

Why the budget changes the estimate.

Eq. (29) mixes the empirical action distribution with a uniform distribution of weight K​α/(N+K​α)K\alpha/(N+K\alpha). For a 30-action menu with α=0.5\alpha=0.5, this weight is 48.4% at N=16N=16 and 1.44% at N=1024N=1024. Larger action budgets reduce this distortion, while more occupancy samples stabilize the aggregate estimate. On the test configurations of Table 12, increasing the budget reduces prediction RMSE from 0.011320.01132 to 0.002300.00230. The selected budget uses about 119 times as many actor queries on calibration.

F.6 Independent Prediction of Deployment Outcomes

Tasks and checkpoints.

The prediction study uses the fixed test set in Table 5, with 576 tasks divided equally across the three MiniWoB++ families. Estimator calibration uses a separate set of 72 tasks, 24 per family, generated in the same way as the splits in Table 5 and disjoint from all of them. This set is fixed before estimator selection and plays no role in the reported test results. We use the H0 checkpoint at post-training update 1,024 and the H1-adapted checkpoints from Appendix F.3. All weights are frozen for this study. The control objective uses γ=0.95\gamma=0.95, τ=0.1\tau=0.1, and a horizon of ten model decisions.

Execution and encoding sweep.

Both final checkpoints are deployed through H0’s native action menu. We cross execution settings with three encodings: the canonical presentation R0, reversed top-level observation fields R1, and a cyclic permutation of action codes R3. The encodings preserve the semantic actions and their execution. The reference is the frozen base model’s distribution under R0, aligned to the same semantic actions in all three presentations. Prompts are held fixed across execution settings and omit numerical reliability and cost values.

The baseline has click reliability p=0.8p=0.8, click cost c=0.01c=0.01, and encoding R0. One sweep varies p∈{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.75,0.8,0.85,0.9,0.95,1}p\in\{0.5,0.6,0.7,0.75,0.8,0.85,0.9,0.95,1\} at fixed c=0.01c=0.01. A second varies c∈{0,0.0025,0.005,0.0075,0.01,0.015,0.02,0.03,0.05}c\in\{0,0.0025,0.005,0.0075,0.01,0.015,0.02,0.03,0.05\} at fixed p=0.8p=0.8. Failed clicks leave the physical page unchanged and consume the decision and its cost. Submission retains the native task semantics. Calibration uses p∈{0.5,0.8,1}p\in\{0.5,0.8,1\} and c∈{0,0.01,0.05}c\in\{0,0.01,0.05\} in their respective sweeps. Crossing these settings with the encodings gives 15 calibration and 36 test configurations per checkpoint. The two checkpoints yield 72 test comparisons with their respective baselines.

Prediction and scoring.

For each task and configuration, an oracle solves the control problem for CC and the queried optimal action distributions. The predictor obtains independent pilot trajectories and finite categorical samples from the deployed policy. Eq. (11) gives M^\widehat{M} for the candidate and baseline. Their predicted return difference is

Δ​J^=Δ​C−Δ​M^.\widehat{\Delta J}=\Delta C-\Delta\widehat{M}. (30)

Appendix F.5 specifies the estimator and calibration. All test predictions are saved before scoring starts. The scoring process computes exact JJ and occupancy-weighted KL from full policy probabilities. The predictor’s data access is limited to samples, pilot states, the reference, oracle ceilings, and queried optimal targets.

Adaptation comparisons.

We evaluate the saved H1-adapted checkpoints at 0, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, and 1,024 updates under native H0 and H1. Each interface retains its frozen base-model reference. At every node, the predictor estimates the recovery difference J⁡(θt,H1)−J⁡(θ0,H0)J(\theta_{t},\mathrm{H1})-J(\theta_{0},\mathrm{H0}) and the ranking difference J⁡(θt,H1)−J⁡(θt,H0)J(\theta_{t},\mathrm{H1})-J(\theta_{t},\mathrm{H0}). The source H0 baseline receives an independent measurement whose cost is included.

Baselines and access.

Ceiling-only prediction sets Δ​M^=0\Delta\widehat{M}=0. The frequency rollout baseline estimates regularized returns directly, using repeated queries at each visited state to estimate the selected action’s log probability. Calibration selects 64 such samples per decision with additive smoothing α=0.5\alpha=0.5. This baseline receives the same actor-query allowance as the diagnostic, including its pilot queries and baseline measurement. Reference computation and oracle construction are recorded separately from actor queries.

Prediction results.

Figure 9 compares predicted and observed return changes across the configuration sweep. Table 12 reports errors in aggregate return differences, where each comparison first averages returns equally across task families. In the configuration sweep, the mismatch-based prediction identifies the direction of all 70 changes outside a 0.010.01 tie region and orders all 1,195 configuration pairs outside that region within each checkpoint. Classifying changes as harmful, tied, or beneficial gives 71 correct predictions out of 72.

In the adaptation study, at the final update 1,024, the exact recovery and ranking differences are 0.008440.00844 and 0.044910.04491, with intervals in Table 9. Their predictions are 0.005790.00579 with 95% interval [−0.00116,0.01228][-0.00116,0.01228] and 0.041950.04195 with interval [0.03371,0.05015][0.03371,0.05015]. Using the same 0.010.01 tie region, three-class predictions agree with the exact values at six of seven recovery nodes and all seven ranking nodes. Figure 5 in Section 6.2 shows the predicted and observed trajectories.

Uncertainty and resources.

We average within each family and give equal weight to the three families. Intervals use 2,000 paired task bootstrap resamples within families. They describe task-sampling uncertainty for the fixed checkpoints. Finite action samples are simulated from cached distributions of the actual language-model checkpoints. The new probability measurements took 2.19 GPU-hours.

F.7 Coding-Agent Harness Study

Harnesses and benchmark.

The study uses the native configurations of DeepAgents, Pi coding-agent, DeepSeek Harness, Terminus-2, and mini-SWE-agent. All file and command tools run inside the benchmark task container. The framework owns its loop, tool feedback, delegation where configured, compression, retries, and termination. Terminus-2 retains tmux, completion confirmation, and summarization. Mini-SWE-agent uses its official tool-call profile. Terminal-Bench Lite contains 39 tasks, scored by the official verifier. The agent never sees scoring data or gold patches.

Accuracy.

Each harness has three independent runs. Accuracy is the mean of the three single-run success rates over all planned tasks, and the reported spread is the sample standard deviation across runs. Timeouts and failures remain in the denominator as unresolved tasks.

Models and budgets.

The target is Qwen3.5-9B with thinking enabled, temperature 0.6, an output limit of 32,768 tokens, and a context window of 65,536 tokens. The teacher is GPT-5.6-luna with the same output and context limits and high reasoning effort. Each trajectory is capped at 50 top-level decisions and uses the task’s own time limit.

Recorded states and sampling.

At each model call, we record the request context, tool definitions, controller state, and remaining budgets. Summary, subagent, and retry calls count as decisions. To sample a decision, we resend the recorded request and decode each sample with the harness’s parser, without executing tools. Samples measure the next action distribution at the recorded state.

Probe tasks and trajectories.

The probes use three Terminal-Bench Lite tasks: acl-permissions-inheritance, analyze-access-logs, and bank-trans-filter. For each harness, the target and the teacher each contribute three trajectories per task, taken from separate runs of their own. A trajectory enters an estimate only when every recorded state in it has a complete probe. The teacher estimates use 7 of 9 trajectories for Pi coding-agent and all 9 for the other harnesses. The target estimates use 7, 6, and 8 of 9 trajectories for Pi coding-agent, DeepAgents, and DeepSeek Harness, and all 9 for Terminus-2 and mini-SWE-agent.

Common action categories.

Each decoded output maps to one of 13 categories: inspect, modify, verify, setup, run, plan, delegate, wait, stop, context update, return, opaque, and invalid. File reads, listings, and searches map to inspect, and writes, edits, and deletions to modify. Todo and planning operations map to plan, and subagent calls to delegate. Shell commands, including Terminus-2 keystrokes at a shell prompt, are parsed, and a command maps to its dominant operation. Commands whose program the parser cannot resolve map to opaque, and responses without a countable native action map to invalid. The categories merge actions with different arguments and effects, so the estimates compare decisions at the level of these categories.

Estimators.

At a recorded state ss under harness hh, let ph(⋅∣s)p_{h}(\cdot\mid s) and qh(⋅∣s)q_{h}(\cdot\mid s) be the target’s and the teacher’s category distributions, estimated from 128 and 64 samples with a pseudocount of 0.50.5 per category. The objective uses the reference php_{h}, a binary terminal reward YY, and no discount. The ceiling estimate averages the teacher’s regularized return over its complete trajectories s0,…,sL−1s_{0},\ldots,s_{L-1}:

C~h=𝔼qh[Y−τ∑t=0L−1KL(qh(⋅∣st)∥ph(⋅∣st))].\widetilde{C}_{h}=\mathbb{E}_{q_{h}}\Bigl[Y-\tau\sum_{t=0}^{L-1}\mathrm{KL}\bigl(q_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\,\big\|\,p_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\bigr)\Bigr]. (31)

The mismatch estimate applies Proposition 6.1 with qhq_{h} in place of the optimum. Without discounting, the factor 1/(1−γ)1/(1-\gamma) becomes a sum over the decisions of each complete target trajectory:

M~h=14​τ​𝔼ph​[∑t=0L−1‖τ​P⟂​log⁡ph(⋅∣st)qh(⋅∣st)‖22].\widetilde{M}_{h}=\frac{1}{4\tau}\,\mathbb{E}_{p_{h}}\Bigl[\sum_{t=0}^{L-1}\Bigl\|\tau P_{\!\perp}\log\frac{p_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{t})}{q_{h}(\cdot\mid s_{t})}\Bigr\|_{2}^{2}\Bigr]. (32)

We use τ=0.1\tau=0.1. With php_{h} as the reference, the target’s regularized return equals its success probability, so the exact ceiling minus mismatch also equals it. The estimates put a teacher that need not be optimal in place of the optimum, so C~h\widetilde{C}_{h} estimates a lower bound on the ceiling and M~h\widetilde{M}_{h} measures distance to the teacher. We therefore compare the ordering of C~h−M~h\widetilde{C}_{h}-\widetilde{M}_{h} with the ordering of accuracy. The mismatch per decision in Figure 6 is M~h\widetilde{M}_{h} divided by the mean number of decisions per complete target trajectory. Table 13 lists the three estimates and the decisions per trajectory, and Figure 10 plots the estimates against accuracy.

Action shares.

Table 14 gives the mean share of each category at the recorded states of complete target trajectories, for the target and for the teacher sampled at the same states. The remaining categories each hold at most 7.2% for either model. Across all five harnesses, the target inspects more often than the teacher. It also marks the task complete less often, except under Terminus-2, where the two do so at similar rates.

F.8 Exact Harness Scores and Task Success

Tasks and harnesses.

We evaluate H0–H5 from Table 4 on the fixed test set of 576 tasks, with 192 tasks from each of the three MiniWoB++ families in Appendix F.1. We reuse their compiled execution graphs, whose transitions and successful task completion were checked against the native browser. The horizon is ten actor decisions, with remaining budget included in the state. H4 retains the archived decisions of its separate frozen Qwen3.5-2B reviewer.

Frozen model and semantic policy.

The actor is off-the-shelf Qwen3.5-9B, with fixed weights and no project adapter. Each prompt exposes the harness’s complete legal action menu, with a single-token code for every parameterized semantic action. We obtain the action distribution by normalizing the corresponding token logits at temperature one, using BF16 inference, FP64 normalization, and a state microbatch of eight. Thinking is disabled. The objective instruction asks the model to maximize exact task completion within its decision budget. Actor probabilities are computed anew for this model under every harness. We set each harness’s reference to this same frozen semantic distribution and hold it fixed when solving for the optimal policy.

Objective and exact computation.

We use the finite-horizon counterpart of Eq. (2), with γ=1\gamma=1, τ=0.1\tau=0.1, binary terminal success reward, and zero explicit execution costs. This objective and reference define a new control problem for each harness, so the ceilings differ from those of the post-training study in Section 3.2. Backward induction on the acyclic graph gives Πℐ∗\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}} and the initial-state optimal value CC. Let νℐΠ​(s)=∑t=09PrℐΠ⁡(st=s)\nu^{\Pi}_{\mathcal{I}}(s)=\sum_{t=0}^{9}\Pr_{\mathcal{I}}^{\Pi}(s_{t}=s) be the expected number of visits to a nonterminal state. Forward propagation under the evaluated policy supplies these visitation weights, giving

M(θ,ℐ)=τ∑sνℐΠθ,ℐ(s)KL(Πθ,ℐ(⋅∣s)∥Πℐ∗(⋅∣s)).M(\theta,\mathcal{I})=\tau\sum_{s}\nu^{\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}}_{\mathcal{I}}(s)\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\Pi_{\theta,\mathcal{I}}(\cdot\mid s)\middle\|\Pi^{*}_{\mathcal{I}}(\cdot\mid s)\right). (33)

The Bellman residual telescopes over the finite horizon to give C−J=MC-J=M. Since the evaluated policy equals its fixed reference, its regularization penalty is zero, and JJ equals task success probability. We compute JJ by forward reward accumulation and success by a separate backward recursion. These independent computations agree with C−MC-M to numerical precision. The largest observed identity residual is 7.22×10−167.22\times 10^{-16}.

Rollout evaluation and aggregation.

For each task and harness, we draw 256 independent trajectories from the measured actor distribution on the compiled graph. The fraction that reaches native task success supplies the vertical coordinate in Figure 11.

Scores and success are averaged within each family and then equally across families. Each point therefore compares the same task distribution. The three selection rules maximize CC, −M-M, and C−MC-M, respectively. The dashed lines are unweighted linear fits through the six displayed harness means. All actor evaluations run on four RTX 4090 GPUs.

For these deterministic task graphs with binary terminal reward, an individual task’s reference success probability SS gives C=τ​log⁡(1+S⁡(e1/τ−1))C=\tau\log(1+S(e^{1/\tau}-1)). This is increasing in SS, but averaging this nonlinear quantity across tasks can order harnesses differently from averaging success. In the aggregate comparison, ceiling selects H0, while both negative mismatch and C−MC-M select H3. Negative mismatch ranks H1 above H0, whereas exact and sampled success rank H0 above H1. Combining ceiling and mismatch gives the complete ordering of the exact mean success probabilities.
